subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 1.5 Motion in Two or Three Dimensions

questions.q: On a winter morning the air temperature is −5 °C, and a cart rolling along a straight track has velocity component v_x = −5 m/s, where the +x direction points east. Which statement is correct?
options: The temperature is a vector; its minus sign gives it a direction, as for v_x.
The cart's speed is −5 m/s, since speed and velocity are the same quantity.
The cart must be west of the origin, because its velocity component is negative.
The temperature is a scalar; its minus sign shows only a value below 0 °C.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any quantity that can be negative is a vector picks this. A temperature has no direction in space; its minus sign only places it below 0 °C on the scale.
A student who treats speed and velocity as the same quantity picks this. Speed is a scalar, the magnitude of the velocity, and is never negative: the cart's speed is 5 m/s.
A student who reads the sign of a velocity component as the side of the origin picks this. A negative v_x means the cart is moving west; it can be east or west of the origin.

Temperature has no direction in space, so it is a scalar. Its minus sign places the value below the zero of the Celsius scale; it does not point anywhere. The cart's −5 m/s, by contrast, is a velocity component whose sign does show a direction: west.
questions.explain: Temperature has no direction in space, so it is a scalar. Its minus sign places the value below the zero of the Celsius scale; it does not point anywhere. The cart's −5 m/s, by contrast, is a velocity component whose sign does show a direction: west.
questions.working: Temperature has no direction in space: scalar; −5 °C is a value below the zero of the scale. v_x = −5 m/s: velocity component, sign gives direction (west); speed = |v_x| = 5 m/s; the sign of v_x says nothing about the cart's position.

questions.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
options: position, speed, acceleration
distance, velocity, acceleration
temperature, position, velocity
displacement, velocity, acceleration
optionWhy: A student who treats speed as the same quantity as velocity picks this. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, a scalar with no direction.
A student who treats distance as the same quantity as displacement picks this. Distance is the length of the path traveled, a scalar with no direction.
A student who thinks a quantity that can be negative must be a vector picks this. Temperature can be below zero, but it has no direction in space, so it is a scalar.
Displacement, velocity and acceleration each have a magnitude and a direction, so all three are vectors.
questions.explain: Displacement, velocity and acceleration each have a magnitude and a direction, so all three are vectors.
questions.working: Vectors: position, displacement, velocity, acceleration. Scalars: distance, speed, temperature.

questions.q: The position vector of a point is r⃗ = (3.0î + 4.0ĵ) m, and r̂ is the unit vector in the direction of r⃗. Which statement about r̂ is correct?
options: It is r⃗ itself, with the same magnitude, unit and direction as r⃗.
It has magnitude 1 m, so its unit is the meter, like that of r⃗.
It has magnitude 1, has no unit, and points the same way as r⃗.
It points along x or y, whichever axis lies closer to r⃗'s direction.
optionWhy: A student who treats a vector and its unit vector as interchangeable picks this. r̂ = r⃗/|r⃗| keeps only the direction: its magnitude is 1, not 5.0 m.
A student who takes 'unit vector' to mean a vector one meter long picks this. Dividing r⃗ by its magnitude cancels the meter, so r̂ has magnitude 1 and no unit.
r̂ = r⃗/|r⃗| = (3.0î + 4.0ĵ) m/(5.0 m) = 0.60î + 0.80ĵ. Dividing by the magnitude leaves magnitude 1 and cancels the meter, and the direction is that of r⃗.
A student who thinks the only unit vectors are î, ĵ and k̂ picks this. r̂ points exactly along r⃗, at an angle between the axes here: r̂ = 0.60î + 0.80ĵ.
questions.explain: r̂ = r⃗/|r⃗| = (3.0î + 4.0ĵ) m/(5.0 m) = 0.60î + 0.80ĵ. Dividing by the magnitude leaves magnitude 1 and cancels the meter, and the direction is that of r⃗.
questions.working: r̂ = r⃗/|r⃗| = (3.0î + 4.0ĵ) m/(5.0 m) = 0.60î + 0.80ĵ: magnitude 1, no unit, same direction as r⃗.

questions.q: The figure shows vectors A⃗ and B⃗ on the left grid and four arrows, P, Q, R and S, on the right grid; both grids have the same scale. Which arrow represents A⃗ + B⃗?
options: Arrow P
Arrow Q
Arrow R
Arrow S
optionWhy: A student who draws A⃗ and B⃗ from one point and joins their heads picks this: arrow P (5 right, 2 down) is A⃗ − B⃗. The sum needs B⃗'s tail at A⃗'s head, which gives 3 right and 4 up.
Placing the tail of B⃗ at the head of A⃗, the resultant runs from the tail of A⃗ to the head of B⃗: (4 − 1) squares right and (1 + 3) squares up, 3 right and 4 up. Arrow Q is that vector.

A student who closes the head-to-tail chain by drawing back to the start picks this: arrow R (3 left, 4 down) is −(A⃗ + B⃗). The resultant points from the first tail to the last head, 3 right and 4 up.

A student who ignores the leftward direction of B⃗'s horizontal part, adding it as if it pointed right, picks this: 4 + 1 = 5 right and 4 up is arrow S. B⃗ goes 1 square left, so the sum goes 4 − 1 = 3 squares right.
questions.explain: Placing the tail of B⃗ at the head of A⃗, the resultant runs from the tail of A⃗ to the head of B⃗: (4 − 1) squares right and (1 + 3) squares up, 3 right and 4 up. Arrow Q is that vector.
questions.working: Reading the left grid: A⃗ is 4 squares right and 1 up; B⃗ is 1 square left and 3 up. Placing B⃗'s tail at A⃗'s head, the resultant from A⃗'s tail to B⃗'s head is (4 − 1) right and (1 + 3) up = 3 right, 4 up.

questions.q: A student uses the object model to describe a 1200 kg car on a 30 km highway trip. Which statement about this model is correct?
options: It is invalid: a car is much too large an object to be treated as a point.
It is valid: the car becomes a single point, and a point has no mass.
It is valid: the car becomes a single point that has all of the car's mass.
It is invalid: the car's wheels turn, so it cannot be treated as a point.
optionWhy: A student who thinks only small objects can be modeled as points picks this. What matters is whether the size affects the question; a few meters is negligible on a 30 km trip.
A student who thinks a point object has no mass picks this. The object model keeps the object's extensive properties: the point has the car's mass, 1200 kg.

In the object model the car's size, shape and internal configuration are ignored, and the car is treated as a single point that keeps its extensive properties, including its 1200 kg mass. For a 30 km trip the car's size does not matter.
A student who thinks any internal motion rules out the object model picks this. The model ignores internal configuration, including the turning of the wheels.
questions.explain: In the object model the car's size, shape and internal configuration are ignored, and the car is treated as a single point that keeps its extensive properties, including its 1200 kg mass. For a 30 km trip the car's size does not matter.
questions.working: Object model: size, shape and internal configuration ignored; the car becomes one point with its mass, 1200 kg. A car's size is negligible compared with a 30 km trip.

questions.q: Which object is NOT accelerating at the instant described?
options: A car going around a curve in the road at a steady 15 m/s
A cart moving along a straight track at a steady 3 m/s
A ball tossed straight up, at its highest point
A train slowing at a steady rate as it approaches a station
optionWhy: A student who thinks constant speed means no acceleration picks this. On a curve the direction of the velocity changes, so the car is accelerating.
A straight path and a steady speed mean neither the magnitude nor the direction of the velocity is changing, so the cart's acceleration is zero.
A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. At the top the ball's velocity is passing from upward to downward, so it is changing: the ball is accelerating.
A student who thinks only speeding up counts as acceleration picks this. A decreasing speed is a change in velocity, so the train is accelerating.
questions.explain: A straight path and a steady speed mean neither the magnitude nor the direction of the velocity is changing, so the cart's acceleration is zero.
questions.working: Accelerating ⇔ velocity changing in magnitude or direction. Only the cart on a straight track at a steady 3 m/s has constant velocity.

questions.q: A cart moves along a straight track with a velocity that changes continuously. Which statement describes the cart's instantaneous velocity at t = 3.0 s?
options: The value its average velocity approaches as an interval around 3.0 s shrinks to zero
Its average velocity over any interval that starts at 3.0 s, whatever the interval's length
Its position at t = 3.0 s divided by the 3.0 s that have passed since t = 0
The mean of its average velocities over several intervals that include t = 3.0 s
optionWhy: The instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval containing t = 3.0 s approaches zero; for a smooth motion this limit is dx/dt at t = 3.0 s.
A student who thinks any interval gives the instantaneous value picks this. The velocity changes continuously, so averages over long intervals differ from the value at t = 3.0 s.
A student who equates velocity with position divided by clock time picks this. That gives at most an average over 0 to 3.0 s, and only if the cart started at the origin.
A student who takes 'instantaneous' to be a mean of averages picks this. The instantaneous value is the limit the averages approach as the interval shrinks, not their mean.
questions.explain: The instantaneous velocity is the limit of the average velocity as the time interval containing t = 3.0 s approaches zero; for a smooth motion this limit is dx/dt at t = 3.0 s.
questions.working: Instantaneous value = limit of the average value as the time interval around the instant approaches zero.

questions.q: The figure shows the path of a bead that slides along a straight wire lying along an x-axis. The bead starts at P, moves to Q, and then moves to R, where it stops. What is the bead's displacement Δx for the whole trip?
optionWhy: A student who takes displacement to be the distance traveled picks this: 4 m from P to Q plus 9 m from Q to R. Displacement uses only the start and end positions.
A student who subtracts the final position from the initial one picks this: (+2 m) − (−3 m) = +5 m. Δx = x − x_0, so the bead's net change is −5 m, toward −x.
A student who takes the final position as the displacement picks this. The bead started at x = +2 m, not at the origin, so Δx = −3 m − 2 m = −5 m.
Displacement depends only on the start and end: Δx = x − x_0 = (−3 m) − (+2 m) = −5 m. The trip out to Q and back does not affect it.
questions.explain: Displacement depends only on the start and end: Δx = x − x_0 = (−3 m) − (+2 m) = −5 m. The trip out to Q and back does not affect it.
questions.working: x_0 = +2 m (P), x = −3 m (R). Δx = x − x_0 = −3 m − (+2 m) = −5 m. (Distance traveled: 4 m + 9 m = 13 m.)

questions.q: The motion diagram shows the position of a cart at five instants separated by equal time intervals as it moves along a straight track. The dots are numbered in time order, and the +x direction is to the right. Which description of the cart's velocity–time (v_x–t) graph for this motion is correct?
options: A straight line that slopes upward and stays above the t axis
A curve that rises quickly at first and then levels off flat
A straight line sloping down that stays above the t axis
A horizontal straight line that lies just below the t axis
optionWhy: A student who thinks the acceleration points in the direction of motion picks this: the cart moves in +x, so they give it a positive acceleration and a rising graph. The shrinking gaps show the cart slowing, so its acceleration is in −x and the graph slopes down.

A student who draws the position graph when asked for the velocity graph picks this: the cart's position does rise quickly and then level off. The velocity is the slope of that position graph, which decreases steadily, so the v_x–t graph is a falling straight line.

Every gap is to the right, so v_x is positive throughout and the graph stays above the time axis. The gaps (8, 6, 4 and 2 m) shrink by the same 2 m in each equal interval, so v_x falls by equal amounts in equal times: a straight line with negative slope.

A student who draws the acceleration graph in place of the velocity graph picks this: the cart's constant, negative acceleration does give a horizontal line below the axis on an a_x–t graph. The velocity is positive and decreasing, so the v_x–t graph slopes down above the axis.
questions.explain: Every gap is to the right, so v_x is positive throughout and the graph stays above the time axis. The gaps (8, 6, 4 and 2 m) shrink by the same 2 m in each equal interval, so v_x falls by equal amounts in equal times: a straight line with negative slope.
questions.working: Gaps 8, 6, 4, 2 m in equal intervals: moving in +x (v_x > 0 throughout) and the gap falls by 2 m each interval, so v_x decreases by equal amounts in equal times: constant negative a_x. v_x–t graph: straight line sloping down, staying above the t axis.

questions.q: An object is in free fall near Earth's surface; it may be moving upward or downward. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 10 m/s² and take upward as positive. Which statement about the object's motion is correct?
options: Its position changes by 10 m downward in every single second
Its velocity changes by 10 m/s downward in every second
Its acceleration is larger than g if its mass is large
Its speed drops by 10 m/s in each second of flight
optionWhy: A student who reads 10 m/s² as 'moves 10 m each second' picks this. The acceleration fixes the change in velocity per second; the distance covered in each second keeps changing (5 m in the first second after release from rest, then 15 m, 25 m, …).

In free fall the acceleration is g = 10 m/s² downward, whatever the object's mass and whether it is rising or falling. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time, so v_y changes by 10 m/s downward in every second.

A student who thinks heavier objects fall with a greater acceleration picks this. With air resistance negligible, every object near Earth's surface has the same acceleration, g ≈ 10 m/s² downward, whatever its mass.

A student who thinks a negative acceleration always means slowing down picks this, since a_y = −10 m/s². The object slows only while it moves upward; when it moves downward, its velocity and acceleration are both downward and it speeds up.
questions.explain: In free fall the acceleration is g = 10 m/s² downward, whatever the object's mass and whether it is rising or falling. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time, so v_y changes by 10 m/s downward in every second.
questions.working: a_y = −10 m/s² throughout free fall, for any mass and either direction of motion: Δv_y = −10 m/s in each second.

questions.q: At one instant, an object's velocity–time (v_x–t) graph crosses the time axis, and the slope of the graph at that instant is not zero. Which statement about the object at that instant is correct?
options: Its velocity is zero, and so its acceleration is zero as well.
It stays at rest for a short time and then moves on again.
Its velocity is zero, but its acceleration is not zero.
It is passing back through its own starting position now.
optionWhy: A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The acceleration is the slope of the v_x–t graph, which the stem says is not zero; the velocity is passing through zero, not staying there.

A student who thinks an object pauses at a turning point picks this. With a nonzero slope the graph crosses the axis at a single instant, so v_x is zero for that instant only; staying at rest would need the graph to lie along the axis.

The height of the v_x–t graph is zero, so v_x = 0 at that instant. The slope of the graph is the acceleration, and it is not zero: the velocity is changing sign, so the object is reversing direction at that instant.

A student who reads the velocity graph as a position graph picks this, taking the crossing to mean x = 0. The height of a v_x–t graph is the velocity, so the crossing means v_x = 0; where the object is depends on the area under the graph.
questions.explain: The height of the v_x–t graph is zero, so v_x = 0 at that instant. The slope of the graph is the acceleration, and it is not zero: the velocity is changing sign, so the object is reversing direction at that instant.
questions.working: Crossing: v_x = 0. Slope ≠ 0: a_x = dv_x/dt ≠ 0. The object reverses direction instantaneously.

questions.q: A passenger sits in a train moving along a straight, level track at constant velocity. She holds a ball above the floor and releases it from rest relative to herself. Air resistance is negligible. Which describes the path of the falling ball as seen by the passenger and by an observer standing beside the track?
options: She sees it drop vertically; the observer sees a parabola
She sees it curve rearward; the observer sees it drop vertically
Both of them see it fall straight down a vertical line
Both of them see it follow one and the same parabola
optionWhy: Relative to the passenger the ball starts from rest and accelerates straight down, so she sees a vertical line. Relative to the ground the ball starts with the train's horizontal velocity, keeps it (with air resistance negligible its only acceleration is g, downward) and accelerates downward, so the observer sees a parabola. The ball lands directly below the release point in the train.

A student who thinks a dropped object falls straight down relative to the ground and is left behind by the train picks this. At release the ball already moves forward with the train and keeps that horizontal velocity, so it stays below the passenger's hand as it falls.

A student who thinks a path is the same for every observer, and that a dropped ball falls straight down, picks this. The observer by the track sees the ball move forward with the train's velocity while it falls, so the path the observer sees is a parabola.

A student who treats the ground frame's description as the one every observer shares picks this. In the passenger's frame the ball has no horizontal velocity, so she sees it fall straight down; each frame's description is equally valid.
questions.explain: Relative to the passenger the ball starts from rest and accelerates straight down, so she sees a vertical line. Relative to the ground the ball starts with the train's horizontal velocity, keeps it (with air resistance negligible its only acceleration is g, downward) and accelerates downward, so the observer sees a parabola. The ball lands directly below the release point in the train.
questions.working: Train frame: ball released from rest, acceleration g down → straight down. Ground frame: initial velocity = train's horizontal velocity, acceleration g down → parabola.

questions.q: The diagram shows three vehicles, P, Q and R, moving along a straight road at constant velocities, shown relative to the road. Which ranks the speeds of the three vehicles as measured by an observer riding in vehicle Q, from greatest to least?
options: P > Q > R
P = R > Q
P > R > Q
R > P > Q
optionWhy: A student who takes the speeds measured relative to the road as the speeds every observer measures picks this. The observer in Q moves at 15 m/s east, so the speeds she measures are found by subtracting Q's velocity: 5 m/s for P, 25 m/s for R, 0 for Q.

A student who takes each relative speed as the difference of the speeds, whatever the directions, picks this: 20 − 15 = 5 and 15 − 10 = 5 m/s. R moves west while Q moves east, so their velocities subtract to give 10 + 15 = 25 m/s.

A student who adds the speeds whatever the directions picks this: 20 + 15 = 35 m/s for P and 10 + 15 = 25 m/s for R. P moves in the same direction as Q, so relative to Q its speed is only 20 − 15 = 5 m/s.
Subtract Q's velocity from each, with east positive: P: 20 − 15 = +5 m/s; R: −10 − 15 = −25 m/s; Q: 0. The observer in Q measures speeds of 25 m/s for R, 5 m/s for P and zero for Q.
questions.explain: Subtract Q's velocity from each, with east positive: P: 20 − 15 = +5 m/s; R: −10 − 15 = −25 m/s; Q: 0. The observer in Q measures speeds of 25 m/s for R, 5 m/s for P and zero for Q.
questions.working: Take east +. Relative to Q: v_P − v_Q = 20 − 15 = +5 m/s; v_R − v_Q = −10 − 15 = −25 m/s; v_Q − v_Q = 0. Speeds: R 25 > P 5 > Q 0.

questions.q: An airplane flies with a velocity of magnitude v relative to the air, pointing due north. A steady wind blows toward the east at 0.60v relative to the ground. What is the magnitude of the airplane's velocity relative to the ground?
optionWhy: A student who adds the two speeds picks this: v + 0.60v. Magnitudes add directly only for parallel velocities; these are perpendicular, so they combine by the Pythagorean theorem.

A student who takes the airplane's velocity relative to the air as its velocity relative to the ground picks this, ignoring the wind. The wind carries the air, and the airplane with it, eastward, so the ground velocity is the sum of the two.

The velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of the velocity relative to the air (v north) and the wind's velocity (0.60v east). These are perpendicular, so the magnitude is √(v² + (0.60v)²) = 1.17v ≈ 1.2v, directed east of north.

A student who puts the velocity relative to the air on the hypotenuse of the triangle picks this: √(v² − (0.60v)²) = 0.8v. The velocity relative to the ground is the sum of the two perpendicular velocities, so it is the hypotenuse and is larger than v.
questions.explain: The velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of the velocity relative to the air (v north) and the wind's velocity (0.60v east). These are perpendicular, so the magnitude is √(v² + (0.60v)²) = 1.17v ≈ 1.2v, directed east of north.
questions.working: v⃗_ground = v⃗_air + v⃗_wind: north v, east 0.60v (perpendicular). |v⃗_ground| = √(v² + 0.36v²) = 1.17v ≈ 1.2v.

questions.q: A ball is launched over level ground with speed v₀ at an angle θ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. Which describes the ball's velocity at the highest point of its path?
options: It is zero, since the ball stops for an instant at the top
It is less than v₀ cos θ and is still decreasing
It is horizontal and equal to v₀ cos θ, as at launch
It is horizontal and equal to v₀, the launch speed
optionWhy: A student who thinks every projectile is momentarily at rest at the top picks this. Only v_y is zero there; the ball is still moving horizontally at v₀ cos θ.
A student who thinks the ball's forward motion is gradually used up picks this. With air resistance negligible, v_x does not change, so at the top it still equals v₀ cos θ, and v_y = 0 there.

At the top only the vertical component of velocity is zero. A projectile's acceleration is vertical (a_x = 0), so v_x keeps its launch value v₀ cos θ. The velocity at the top is therefore horizontal with magnitude v₀ cos θ.

A student who treats the whole launch speed as the horizontal velocity picks this, since at the top all of the motion is horizontal. Only the horizontal component of the launch velocity, v₀ cos θ, survives at the top; the vertical component v₀ sin θ has been reduced to zero.
questions.explain: At the top only the vertical component of velocity is zero. A projectile's acceleration is vertical (a_x = 0), so v_x keeps its launch value v₀ cos θ. The velocity at the top is therefore horizontal with magnitude v₀ cos θ.
questions.working: At the top v_y = 0 and v_x = v₀ cos θ (a_x = 0, so unchanged since launch): velocity horizontal, magnitude v₀ cos θ.

questions.q: The diagram (not to scale) shows a ball kicked horizontally off the top of a vertical cliff above level ground. Air resistance is negligible. Use g = 10 m/s². How far from the base of the cliff does the ball land?
optionWhy: A student who uses the launch speed as the initial vertical velocity picks this: 45 = 12t + 5t² gives t ≈ 2.0 s and 12 × 2.0 ≈ 24 m. The launch velocity is horizontal, so its vertical component is zero.

A student who thinks the ball falls 10 m in each second picks this: 45 m ÷ 10 m/s = 4.5 s, and 12 × 4.5 = 54 m. The ball accelerates downward, falling 5 m in the first second, 15 m in the next and 25 m in the third: 45 m in 3.0 s.

A student who thinks the ball's forward motion is used up during the flight picks this: if v_x fell steadily from 12 m/s to zero, the average would be 6 m/s, and 6 × 3.0 = 18 m. A projectile has a_x = 0, so v_x stays 12 m/s.
Treat the components separately. Vertically the ball starts with v_y = 0 and falls 45 m: 45 = (1/2)(10)t², so t = 3.0 s. Horizontally nothing changes v_x = 12 m/s, so Δx = (12 m/s)(3.0 s) = 36 m.
questions.explain: Treat the components separately. Vertically the ball starts with v_y = 0 and falls 45 m: 45 = (1/2)(10)t², so t = 3.0 s. Horizontally nothing changes v_x = 12 m/s, so Δx = (12 m/s)(3.0 s) = 36 m.
questions.working: Vertical: 45 = (1/2)(10)t² → t = 3.0 s. Horizontal: v_x = 12 m/s constant → Δx = 12 × 3.0 = 36 m.

questions.q: A ball is launched from level ground with speed v₀ at 37° above the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.60, cos 37° = 0.80). Air resistance is negligible, and the acceleration due to gravity is g. What is the maximum height the ball reaches?
options: 0.18 v₀²/g
0.32 v₀²/g
0.50 v₀²/g
0.36 v₀²/g
optionWhy: Only the vertical component matters for the height: v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀. At the top v_y = 0, so 0 = (0.60v₀)² − 2gH and H = 0.36v₀²/(2g) = 0.18 v₀²/g.

A student who takes the vertical component as v₀ cos 37° = 0.80v₀ picks this: (0.80v₀)²/(2g) = 0.32 v₀²/g. With the angle measured from the horizontal, the vertical side is opposite the angle, so v_y0 = v₀ sin 37°.
A student who uses the launch speed v₀ as the initial vertical velocity picks this: v₀²/(2g). That is the height for a launch straight up; at 37° only 0.60v₀ of the launch velocity is vertical.

A student who multiplies the initial vertical velocity by the time to the top picks this: (0.60v₀)(0.60v₀/g) = 0.36 v₀²/g. The vertical velocity falls steadily to zero, so the average is half of 0.60v₀, which gives 0.18 v₀²/g.
questions.explain: Only the vertical component matters for the height: v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀. At the top v_y = 0, so 0 = (0.60v₀)² − 2gH and H = 0.36v₀²/(2g) = 0.18 v₀²/g.
questions.working: v_y0 = v₀ sin 37° = 0.60v₀. At the top v_y = 0: 0 = (0.60v₀)² − 2gH → H = 0.36v₀²/(2g) = 0.18 v₀²/g.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the work done on a system by a force exerted on it?
options: Energy transferred into or out of the system by the force as the system moves.
The force exerted on the system multiplied by the time for which it is exerted.
Energy that the force puts inside the system, which the system then contains as work.
The effort needed to exert the force, whether or not the system ever moves at all.
optionWhy: Work is a transfer of energy between a system and its surroundings by a force, and it happens only while the point where the force is exerted moves with a component along the force. Positive work transfers energy in; negative work transfers it out.

A student who thinks work depends on how long a force is exerted picks this. Work is the force component along the displacement times the displacement; time does not appear, and a force on an object that does not move does no work however long it is exerted.

A student who thinks of work as something a system holds picks this. Work is energy in transit; the energy transferred shows up as a form of the system’s energy, such as kinetic energy, not as stored ‘work’.
A student who uses the everyday meaning of work as effort picks this. A force on a system that does not move transfers no energy to it, however tiring the force is to exert.
questions.explain: Work is a transfer of energy between a system and its surroundings by a force, and it happens only while the point where the force is exerted moves with a component along the force. Positive work transfers energy in; negative work transfers it out.

questions.q: Identical blocks are released from rest at the tops of the three frictionless ramps shown and slide to the floor. Which claim correctly compares the work done by gravity on the blocks, from the top of each ramp to the floor?
options: It is greatest on Ramp 3, the longest.
It is greatest on Ramp 1, the steepest.
It is the same on all three ramps.
It is zero: gravity is conservative.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gravity’s work grows with the distance traveled picks this. On a longer ramp the component of gravity along the ramp is smaller, mg sin θ, and over the length h/sin θ it does the same work, mgh.
A student who compares forces instead of work picks this. The component of gravity along Ramp 1 is the largest, but it acts over the shortest distance; the product is mgh on every ramp.

Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions: W_g = mgh for each block, because each drops the same height h. The ramp’s length and steepness change how the work is spread along the path, not its total.
A student who thinks a conservative force does no work picks this. Gravity does positive work mgh on each block as it descends; ‘conservative’ means only that this work does not depend on the path.
questions.explain: Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions: W_g = mgh for each block, because each drops the same height h. The ramp’s length and steepness change how the work is spread along the path, not its total.
questions.working: W_g = (mg sin θ)(L) along a ramp of angle θ and length L = h/sin θ, so W_g = mgh on every ramp. Distractors: longest ramp (Ramp 3) from W = mgL; steepest ramp (Ramp 1) from the largest force component; zero from ‘conservative means no work’.

questions.q: A block attached to a spring slides back and forth along a rough incline. Which of the forces exerted on the block is nonconservative, and why?
options: Kinetic friction: it destroys some of the block’s energy, so energy is not conserved.
Gravity: it changes the block’s kinetic energy, so it does not conserve its energy.
The spring force: it does negative work on the block while the block compresses the spring.
Kinetic friction: its work on the block depends on the length of the path the block takes.
optionWhy: A student who thinks nonconservative forces destroy energy picks this. Friction is nonconservative, but energy is conserved: friction transfers mechanical energy into thermal energy. The defining property is the path dependence of its work.

A student who thinks a conservative force does no work on an object picks this. Gravity does change the block’s kinetic energy, but its work depends only on the change in height, so it is conservative.

A student who thinks a force that does negative work is nonconservative picks this. The spring force does negative work during compression and positive work during extension; its work depends only on the initial and final stretch, so it is conservative.

Kinetic friction always opposes the block’s motion relative to the incline, so its work is −F_f times the path length and depends on the path; it is nonconservative. Gravity and the spring force do work that depends only on the block’s initial and final positions.
questions.explain: Kinetic friction always opposes the block’s motion relative to the incline, so its work is −F_f times the path length and depends on the path; it is nonconservative. Gravity and the spring force do work that depends only on the block’s initial and final positions.
